items.title: ‘People are chucking stuff like gold and Bitcoin’ as rising inflation leads investors to seek yield
items.summary:
Bitcoin’s escape from the trenches didn’t last long. The cryptocurrency fell more than 4% on Friday to $68,500, wiping out gains built over the past three months and casting doubt on whether its bear market was ever really over.

The asset also faces weaker investor appetite, according to crypto analytics provider CryptoQuant. The firm’s demand indicator recorded its weakest reading since December 2023, while Bitcoin exchange-traded funds became net sellers again.

The recent downturn has also extended to other parts of the crypto market. That includes Tether’s USDT, the largest cryptocurrency pegged to the U.S. dollar, whose total value shrank by $7.7 billion over the past two months, according to CryptoQuant, a sign that less cash is available in crypto markets.

This time around, inflation has been the main culprit. Tuesday’s Consumer Price Index report showed prices rose 0.4% in October, more than economists expected. Even stripping out food and energy, inflation ran hotter than forecast. Traders now overwhelmingly expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point in December, with some betting on an even bigger increase.

“Because these are non-yielding assets, and we expect inflation to rise… people are chucking stuff like gold and Bitcoin to find… government bonds that are going up, providing you [with] income,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at financial technology company IG Group, told Fortune .

Bitcoin isn’t alone in its retreat. Gold traded near $3,900 an ounce on Friday, well below its January peak of about $5,600,…

items.title: 5 things Jensen Huang mastered that Nvidia’s next CEO will have to learn
items.summary:
The tech world loves superhuman leaders who can withstand boardroom coups and weather negative publicity. Steve Jobs navigated negative press during his tenure at Apple. Elon Musk’s transgressions are forgiven by his followers because of what he brings to his companies. And Sam Altman survived a boardroom coup a little under three years ago.

Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s one-of-a-kind CEO and figurehead since its founding in 1993, couldn’t survive reports of successive romance scandals. On November 12, he was defenestrated and replaced by his chief financial officer as interim CEO. But in the long term, a permanent replacement will be needed.

Finding the right person will be tricky. Huang was renowned for his attention to detail, larger-than-life leadership style, and outgoing personality. He deftly navigated competing business and geopolitical interests to build one of the world’s most valuable companies—and managed to master a wide range of disciplines along the way.

So what qualities will his successor have to replicate?

Managing geopolitics 

Huang’s downfall began with a dalliance with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, the CEO of tech company Megaspeed. But one of his biggest strengths was his ability to navigate the messy geopolitics of the AI race between the U.S. and China—and the awkward relationship between Taiwan, home to TSMC, which is central to Nvidia’s chipmaking process, and China, which wants to invade it.

“The fact that he was born in Taiwan, is the founder-CEO of Nvidia, and has been able to advocate for less-hawkish approaches to tech policy vis-a-vis…
items.t: 5 things Jensen Huang mastered that Nvidia’s next CEO will have to learn

items.title: Ukraine designed its own national typeface so it doesn’t have to use Russian fonts
items.summary:
Ukraine has had enough of Russian fonts.

Amid the country’s invasion by Russia, Ukrainians will no longer have to read any official documents set in a Russian typeface after a just-unveiled typeface goes into full effect. The new national font is called Zakon, “law” in Ukrainian.

Designers, military personnel, and Ukrainian citizens have for years called for their country to swap out Russian-designed Cyrillic fonts like Izhitsa, which appears on official documents, certificates, awards, diplomas, battle flags, and plaques, according to Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture. Though the Russian font and others are widely used in Ukraine, they’re designed by the Russian type foundry ParaType , which Ukraine’s ministry says cooperates with Russian authorities.

To change that, Ukraine’s government and the country’s largest online jobs board partnered to hire a team of Ukrainian type designers to make something imbued with the country’s typographic heritage. A beta version of the font became available on October 29, and after a feedback period, a refined, expanded version is expected to be released early next year and will appear on official Ukrainian documents.

[Image: Ministry of Culture of Ukraine] 

Ukraine’s parliament adopted a resolution in January to create the country’s own national typeface, saying that it would address the legacy of Russian cultural influence from when Ukraine was part of the Soviet Union .

A team of four Ukrainian type designers designed Zakon, which was unveiled last month in Cyrillic and Latin characters. The designers are Oleksiy Chekal, who designed…
items.t: Ukraine designed its own national typeface so it doesn’t have to use Russian fonts

items.title: Exclusive: OpenAI disbands its stand-alone robotics team as its general models start running robots
items.summary:
OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team, moving its researchers onto other teams.

The company confirmed the reorganization when asked about it by Fortune. A company spokesperson said that robotics remains a core part of OpenAI’s long-term vision and portrayed the reorganization as a sign of the company’s commitment to robotics, rather than a retreat from it.

OpenAI said it has reassigned its robotics research team to the company’s main research team, reporting to Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware teams have been reassigned to the company’s larger Applied organization, which reports to OpenAI President Greg Brockman.

The change came recently enough that OpenAI had already registered a booth at CoRL, a top academic robotics conference in Austin, this week. Though the conference app and floor plan marked OpenAI’s spot, when Fortune visited booth #208, it sat empty with OpenAI’s logo nowhere to be seen. 

OpenAI had a robotics team in its early days but wound it down in 2020, with cofounder Wojciech Zaremba later citing limited robot data and a more efficient path toward artificial general intelligence (AGI)—the human-like AI that has been OpenAI’s goal since its founding—through other methods. In particular, OpenAI became increasingly devoted to training ultra-large language models on vast datasets of human-written text. This is the approach that eventually yielded the company’s breakthrough product ChatGPT in late 2022.

OpenAI rebuilt a stand alone robotics team in 2024, announcing a partnership with the startup Figure…
items.t: Exclusive: OpenAI disbands its robotics team as its general models start running robots

items.title: Forget ‘sponsored’ tags in AI answers. Agent loyalty is what matters
items.summary:
No one loves ads, but generally people will tolerate them if it means getting something free or at a lower price. What people won’t forgive? Being lied to.

A study looking at how consumers see native ads on news sites—which look similar to editorial content, just with labels—found that fewer than 10% of consumers could identify them as advertising. And when people find out after the fact, they don’t take it well. In a Contently survey , two-thirds of readers said they felt deceived when they realized an article or video was sponsored by a brand.

That’s why there’s a whole set of regulations and standards around advertising disclosures that are meant to protect consumers. Now that AI is slowly becoming a central part of our media ecosystem, it’s unclear to what extent those disclosures should carry over into AI answers . After all, if the public is increasingly using AI to shop (47% of U.S. shoppers who use AI started their last product search with AI, according to an impact.com survey , and Meta says shopping is the most common use of its new personal AI agent, Muse ), it feels intuitive that the user should see plainly the commercial interests of the sites that informed any answer.

Truth in labeling? 

A reliable label in AI sounds like a good idea, but it gets complicated quickly. For starters, the label might cause confusion that the AI platform itself was paid rather than the original publisher. In the case of ChatGPT that would potentially conflict with its own ads, which are separate from the answer and labeled as sponsored. OpenAI’s answer to the disclosure…
items.t: Forget ‘sponsored’ tags in AI answers. Agent loyalty is what matters

items.title: How to survive the loss of an irreplaceable leader
items.summary:
The challenge of replacing Jensen Huang, the visionary co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, who resigned yesterday morning amid reports of extramarital affairs, may be daunting—but it is far from unprecedented.

While research shows that companies moving on from a founding CEO face a higher risk of failure or downturn than other CEO transitions, major corporations from Apple to Amazon have successfully managed the loss of a larger-than-life presence at the top of the corporate ladder.

Management experts who have studied such transitions say there are a few key lessons.

Don’t look for a carbon copy of the founder 

When Tim Cook replaced legendary Apple founder Steve Jobs in 2011, speculation suggested he might try to replicate Jobs’ style, right down to the signature turtleneck and jeans. However, experts warned against directly replicating Jobs’ leadership and management style.

“A copy of anyone is going to come off looking bad,” Wharton management professor Peter Cappelli said . “It will never be as good as the original, and people will spend their time focusing on the differences.”

Cook succeeded by building on Apple’s strengths and emphasizing his expertise as an operations specialist, scaling the sophisticated global supply chain he helped build as chief operating officer to increase annual revenue nearly fourfold.

Instead of positioning himself as a visionary like his legendary predecessor, Cook maintained an understated management style and let the company’s massive financial success speak for itself. Cook says he urged his own successor, John Ternus, to take his own…
items.t: How to survive the loss of an irreplaceable leader

items.title: Friday the 13th is here. Its impact on your work day may not be so scary
items.summary:
Business can be risky, so it’s natural that superstitions can sometimes creep in when money and careers are at stake.

This workweek ends on Friday the 13th, so in the Western world, the stage is set for fear to influence commerce. 

Let’s take a look at the so-called bad luck day’s origins and how it impacts the business world.

What is a fear of Friday the 13th called? 

A fear of Friday the 13th is called “paraskevidekatriaphobia,” a term created by psychotherapist Donald Dossey . It combines the Greek words for Friday, 13, and fear.

How many Friday the 13ths are there in a year? 

Around every 212.35 days, a Friday the 13th occurs. This figure is based on a complete 400-year Gregorian calendar cycle. 

Another way to look at it: there is at least one Friday the 13th a year, but there can be up to three. This year, 2026, Friday the 13th will be in triplicate.

When did Friday the 13th become unlucky? 

The truth is, no one really knows how exactly Friday the 13th became synonymous with misfortune. 

There are historical and religious references that might shed some light. One of the theories is that the number 12 is considered perfect and complete, so by comparison, 13 is less than.

A popular retelling of Norse mythology states that 12 gods were having a banquet in Valhalla until Loki showed up uninvited, bringing their numbers to 13. The unwelcome guest was able to trick the blind god Höd into killing his brother Balder.

The number 13 and the day Friday also show up in Christianity. According to Christian teachings, there were 13 people present at the Last Supper,…
items.t: Friday the 13th is here. Its impact on your work day may not be so scary

items.title: Your burnout may be a boundaries issue
items.summary:
Below, Nabeela Elsayed shares five key insights from her new book, Breaking Burnout: How High Achievers Break the Success Myths Driving Exhaustion, Overwork, and Burnout .

Nabeela is a recovering workaholic and former C-suite executive. She began her career as a barista making $6.50 an hour and spent the next 20-plus years climbing the corporate ladder until she ran operations and people at companies including Walmart Canada and IKEA.

What’s the Big Idea? 

Burnout isn’t a stamina problem. It isn’t a boundaries problem. It’s what happens when the definition of success you were handed was never survivable in the first place. Getting off the burnout loop isn’t a dramatic leap. It’s a series of small choices toward a life that no longer costs you yourself.

Listen to the audio version of this Book Bite—read by Nabeela herself—in the Next Big Idea App , or buy the book .

1. Fix your relationship with work, not just your job. 

When I lived in Sweden, I learned about lördagsgodis —Saturday candy. Kids and grown-ups skip sweets all week and enjoy them on Saturdays. This is a country with a pastry shop on every corner, yet an entire society says “not today” six out of seven days. That’s not willpower. Back in the 1940s and 1950s, dental researchers discovered that how often you eat sugar does more damage than how much. Health authorities said: if you’re going to have it, have it once a week. That became a ritual in families.

Sugar is not a villain, and neither is work itself. We need to work, but like food, it can nourish or poison you depending on how often and how intensely…
items.t: Your burnout may be a boundaries issue

items.title: Republicans redrew North Carolina to win nearly two-thirds of its House seats — the blue wave left them poised to hold less than a third
items.summary:
During the 2026 election cycle, Republicans enacted a series of gerrymanders – a form of partisan redistricting – in a handful of states to give them a disproportionate edge over Democrats in their congressional delegations. Democrats responded with a successful redistricting effort in California and an unsuccessful one in Virginia .

Gerrymandering has obvious implications for fairness and democracy, characterized by some as politicians picking their voters, not voters picking their politicians.

There’s also a practical consideration for those doing the gerrymandering: The efforts can fail when they overplay their hand.

By spreading their supportive voters across many districts, parties can create more seats that may lean in their direction. But if spread too thin, these efforts can backfire and net seats for the other party, particularly in a “wave” election year that favors the other party. This unintended consequence is often referred to as a “dummymander .”

So, with such massive Democratic majorities poised to enter the 120th Congress, did Republican attempts to gerrymander actually end up costing them some seats in the U.S. House?

The answer isn’t as clear-cut as you might think.

Dummymanders in North Carolina and Ohio? 

Republican state legislatures in Ohio and North Carolina redrew their congressional maps in 2025 , crafting a set of districts they believed would maximize the number of seats they could win in the House.

Despite both states being traditionally competitive in statewide elections, their state legislatures drew a collection of seats Republicans…
items.t: Republicans redrew North Carolina to win nearly two-thirds of its House seats — the blue wave left them poised to hold less than a third

items.title: The Jensen Huang Nvidia affair recalls China’s ‘beauty stratagem’ that dates back 2,000 years
items.summary:
Extramarital activities have led to the resignation of one of America’s most influential tech bosses, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The saga has also raised the specter of an age-old spying tactic: the “honey trap.”

Huang stepped down following media reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence agencies . She previously worked for Megaspeed, a cloud computing company under U.S. scrutiny for allegedly helping China obtain restricted AI chips.

Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair . And amid reports of a second with a company executive who reports to him , he tendered his resignation to the Nvidia board on Nov. 12, 2026.

The sensitivity of Huang’s work – AI is increasingly seen as central to national security – has turned a company matter into an international issue. China’s Foreign Ministry has denied the espionage allegations and accused the U.S. of “fabricating so-called spy narratives and ⁠⁠⁠⁠using them as a pretext for imposing ⁠⁠⁠⁠a technological blockade.” Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets have been leaked.

Yet part of what makes the accusations so believable is history is dotted with examples of men being distracted, compromised or spied on by attractive men and women deployed for that purpose.

Indeed, in China it recalls an ancient political tactic known as “meiren ji” or the “ beauty stratagem .”

As a scholar specializing in U.S.-China relations , I believe that regardless of the particulars of the Huang case, the political logic behind the beauty…
items.t: The Jensen Huang Nvidia affair recalls China’s ‘beauty stratagem’ that dates back 2,000 years

“I believe so,” Wong said after an AAPA conference when asked whether high airfares would become a lasting feature rather than a temporary adjustment. “We are living in completely different market conditions and a completely different cost environment … and it looks like these high prices will continue to prevail.”

On whether airlines could implement another round of fare increases if fuel prices remain high, Wong said there was no clear answer as passenger price sensitivity varies across markets.

Major airlines across the Asia-Pacific, Europe and North America have raised base fares, hiked fuel surcharges or added extra fees since the Iran war began in late February.

items.title: This Houston startup is using old oil wells to make clean hydrogen
items.summary:
Deep in West Texas, an old oil field is nearing the end of its commercial life. But a startup recently spent a month at the site producing a new energy source: clean, ultra low-carbon hydrogen.

Eclipse , the startup, uses microbes to break down oil in end-of-life wells, releasing hydrogen that can be brought to the surface using existing infrastructure. In the pilot, the company generated hydrogen for 30 days straight before stopping the test. But the company says that old oil field projects like this have the potential to produce hydrogen for 10-20 years—and can make it cheap enough that it could be used to produce clean, baseload power for the electric grid.

There’s an abundant supply of hydrogen in oil fields. “When you produce these oil fields, you’re lucky if you produce 40% of the oil,” says Eclipse’s CEO, Prabhdeep Singh Sekhon, who previously worked in the oil and gas industry. “There’s still a tremendous amount of hydrocarbon in the ground; it’s just not economic to produce. If there’s hydrocarbon, that also inherently means there’s also hydrogen.”

Mining old oil fields for clean energy 

Other approaches to clean hydrogen have struggled. The promise is big: Hydrogen emits only water vapor when it’s burned, and it could slash emissions in everything from steel production to ships . But it’s hard to make affordably. Green hydrogen, which uses renewable electricity to split water, is expensive and water intensive. Hydrogen is traditionally made with natural gas, and it’s also expensive to capture carbon in that approach. “Natural” or geologic hydrogen, which…
items.t: This Houston startup is using old oil wells to make clean hydrogen

What’s happened? 

Shortly after noon ET yesterday, November 12, people around the world began reporting that they could not access the Outlook email service, as well as some other Microsoft services that interact with Exchange Online, like Teams.

For the first few hours, those on social media joked that this was a nice break from work . After all, Outlook is one of the largest business email platforms in the world, and when it goes down, a large part of an employee’s workflow goes down with it.

But as the hours dragged on with no Outlook access restored, the outage started becoming a major issue worldwide—and not just for businesses. Any entity that uses Outlook services, including government agencies, hospitals, emergency services, and schools, was also being impacted.

Fast forward to this morning, and Microsoft has restored access to some of its services (like Teams), but the Outlook outage is still ongoing. 

Such a long service interruption is rare for a platform as critical for communications and as large as Outlook—especially one run by a nearly $4 trillion company with nearly unlimited technical resources at its disposal.

What caused the outage?

The new Ford World HQ opened in November 2025 as a 21st-century expression of the Ford Rouge logic, according to Ford Land CEO Jim Dobleske. World HQ stacks modern teams vertically the way Henry Ford stacked steel and assembly at the Rouge. It used to take 30 minutes to move a car from one end of the old design center to the other; now it takes “just over three minutes.” The birdsong in the courtyard is piped in, predator calls included, to keep Michigan’s ever-present geese away from workers wolfing down their lunches. “Those are not real birds,” Dobleske said, “that’s all fake.”

Fortune visited Ford in 1947 to document the “rebirth” of the company, when founder Henry Ford died and his grandson, Henry Ford II, was leading the postwar modernization of the iconic American manufacturer. items.title: Yuri Suzuki’s ‘Onomatopia’ is a mini theme park designed to be listened to
items.summary:
Sound artist, designer, and electronic musician Yuri Suzuki uses ambient noise and miniature rides inspired by theme park attractions to explore the connections between play, sound, and architecture in his new exhibition Onomatopia .

On display through January 7, 2027, in the Osh Gallery at Pentagram’s London headquarters, the exhibition includes five dioramas based on amusement park attractions, world fairs, and expos. It’s a prototype of a theme park built around one’s sense of hearing, as each ride makes its own specific noises. The park in total is designed to evoke a greater appreciation for the role of sound.

Suzuki is a former Pentagram partner who designed a logo for the musical standard MIDI that’s both visual and sonic, and his Ambient Machine lets you customize your own white noise . He’s also designed public multisensory artwork, including for the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and a Sonic Playground for Atlanta’s High Museum of Art.

Suzuki’s latest work continues to explore those ideas. There’s a mini roller coaster called “Harmony in Motion” with horns in red, yellow, blue, and green in varying heights sprouting around the tracks, which sound like an organ playing in harmony. A red, yellow, and blue Ferris wheel display named “Mechanical Music Wheel” makes the sound of bright rising and falling chimes.

[Photo: Courtesy Pentagram] 

A bumper cars attraction makes irregular plucking sounds. And there’s a sonic carousel and helter-skelter, each made from multicolored horns. Suzuki tells Fast Company he tends to use primary colors because they are…
items.t: Yuri Suzuki’s ‘Onomatopia’ is a mini theme park designed to be listened to

items.title: The war on polyester is coming for your underwear. One brand’s answer? Wool
items.summary:
Back when she was too young to buy her own clothes, Kerry O’Brien remembers loathing hefty wool sweaters—especially turtlenecks. But her career as the founder and CEO of basics brand Commando gave her a new perspective on fabrics and fibers, including a love for wool and what can be done with it beyond creating itchy knitwear. Now, decades after her turtleneck terrors, O’Brien brought wool to unexpected new territory: panties. 

Commando started out nearly 25 years ago by transferring some of the fabrics engineered for activewear to women’s intimates, originally building a brand on seamless, raw-cut panties made of a synthetic fabric. But the new wool panties , which are available online now and in select stores and retail for $38, inherently achieve a lot of what those nylon panties do artificially. 

“Nothing can really replicate the technical aspects of wool , what it does naturally,” O’Brien tells Fast Company . 

This wool underwear debut coincidentally comes amid some consumers’ growing war on polyester, which also happens to be the most produced fiber on the planet.

[Photo: Commando] 

Abercrombie, for instance, recently drew controversy online over a mostly synthetic women’s sweater marketed as a “wool-blend.” More broadly, a growing number of fashion content creators are lauding the benefits of natural fibers over synthetics, citing environmental and health concerns . (So are wellness and MAHA influencers, although a direct, causal connection between microplastics and sickness has yet to be proven ). “Polyester” has even become an insult among Gen Z.

items.t: The war on polyester is coming for your underwear. One brand’s answer? Wool

items.title: How Novig became the third biggest prediction market site despite launching only months ago
items.summary:
Since bursting on the scene two years ago, prediction markets have become one of the buzziest new sectors in finance, pulling in billions of dollars in revenue, and driving daily news headlines. The young industry is dominated by two giants, Kalshi and Polymarket, but numerous other companies are trying to muscle into the field. That includes the sports-focused prediction market Novig, which only launched as a federally regulated prediction market in August, but has already claimed the number three spot by one widely used industry metric.

Over the past 30 days, Novig handled $1.8 billion in trading volume on U.S.-regulated exchanges, according to the PM Pulse, a newsletter that tracks prediction market volume using data from research firm Aldrin. That figure is small next to Kalshi’s $33.3 billion and Polymarket U.S.’s $6.3 billion. But it’s about $300 million ahead of Crypto.com, the fourth-place contender, and its volume is up 80% from the previous 30 days.

The volume figures don’t account for combos, or multi-game parlays, which Sam Schwartz, who runs the newsletter, says can inflate volume without producing proportionally more revenue for the exchange. 

Novig’s ascent is notable given how little money it has raised compared to other prediction markets. Founded in 2021, the company enjoyed modest growth and raised $30 million as it pursued a sweepstakes-based business model that allowed it to operate in certain states. But a shift in the legal landscape led Novig this year to become a federally regulated prediction market, helping it raise a new $75 million Series B…
items.t: How Novig became the third biggest prediction market site despite launching only months ago

items.title: Jane Street more than doubled its Nvidia stake last quarter, filings reveal
items.summary:
Jane Street, one of Wall Street’s leading quantitative trading firms, more than doubled its Nvidia holdings in the third quarter, according to regulatory filings released Thursday and reviewed by Fortune. The securities filings show the firm’s positions as of Sept. 30—just over six weeks before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The scandal has led Nvidia shares to fall nearly 13% over the past five days, reaching a 17-month low intraday Thursday. The regulatory disclosure, known as a 13F, doesn’t reveal exactly when Jane Street purchased the shares, or how much the firm has gained or lost on its bets though.

The market maker held 23.8 million shares worth about $5.44 billion at $228.38 at quarter end, according to the 13F. That’s over double the 11.8 million shares held, worth $2.4 billion, in the second quarter. Nvidia was its second-largest holding behind SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust. Jane Street declined Fortune ’s request for comment. 

The filings show what Jane Street held in late September, not what it owns now, and leave out short positions. Jane Street traders could, in theory, have shorted Nvidia after the reporting period ended and made money from the subsequent decline. The filings alone cannot tell us whether they did, though.

Options add another layer of complexity to this. The 13F also discloses that Jane Street holds a large amount of puts and calls, which are reported using the value of the underlying shares, rather than the market value of the…
items.t: Jane Street more than doubled its Nvidia stake last quarter, filings reveal

items.title: Nvidia’s new chairman Harvey Jones is a ‘charming elder statesman’ set to lead the search for the next CEO. But did he enable the current crisis?
items.summary:
In the wake of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s stunning departure from the company, employees received an email from someone most of them had probably never heard of before, even though he’d been affiliated with the company and its board for decades. His name is Harvey Jones, and he was writing to tell them that he’d just been appointed the company’s first-ever Chair of the Board, and that Nvidia CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO.

“I’m writing to share an important update,” Jones’ note began, according to leaked screenshots of the email. He then tried to reassure employees no doubt left shaken by the past weeks’ revelations and the sudden departure of Jensen Huang, a man who co-founded the company and, until today, had been synonymous with its success. “The Board takes seriously our duty as steward of this great company,” Jones said.

That sense of calm and confidence is something Jones is known for, according to two longtime friends and former coworkers. Although Jones, 73, may not be a household name, he has worked in the technology industry, and in semiconductors, for over 30 years, according to his biography on the Nvidia website. He founded two companies, served as CEO of another, and since 2004 has been managing partner of investment firm Square Wave Ventures. He’s been on Nvidia’s board since 1993, the year Huang founded the company.

Jones comes from a successful Connecticut family—his full name is Harvey Jones III—with an “old school, conservative” way about him, Penny Herscher, who has known Jones since 1984 and used to work for him, tells Fortune .…
items.t: Nvidia’s new chairman Harvey Jones is a ‘charming elder statesman’ set to lead the search for the next CEO. But did he enable the current crisis?

items.title: Will AI change banking more in the next five years than the past 30? UAE lenders think so
items.summary:
Banking in the UAE is approaching an inflection point as AI begins to reshape everything from customer service and compliance to cybersecurity and internal operations. 

Developments highlighted at last week’s Dubai FinTech Summit 2026 suggest that the country’s largest lenders are no longer simply experimenting with AI but preparing to make it a fundamental part of how they operate.

Emirates NBD, Dubai’s largest lender by assets , shared how it has more than 150 AI initiatives underway, with 65 already in production.

The bank, which is majority government-owned, has been aggressively scaling its digital transformation by committing approximately 50% of its technology budget to AI.

In June, Emirates NBD was ranked the most AI-advanced bank in the Middle East & Africa (MEA) based on an analysis of publicly available data from 25 banks across the region. 

According to Evident, a London-based market intelligence firm which compiled the ranking, Emirates NBD “explicitly” links AI to enterprise productivity, operational modernisation and the UAE’s national AI agenda.

Other GCC banks included in the ranking were First Abu Dhabi Bank (#3), Saudi Arabia’s Al Rajhi (#9) and Dubai’s Mashreq (#10).

Last month, Emirates NBD became the first bank in the MENA region to deploy OpenAI’s GPT models using local, in-country infrastructure. This allows it to run advanced LLMs at scale while meeting strict UAE data residency, privacy, and regulatory compliance laws.

The bank plans to integrate OpenAI’s models across its operations to enhance customer experiences, strengthen risk…
items.t: Will AI change banking more in the next five years than the past 30? UAE lenders think so
